title: Rules vs Learning - How Each System Works
summary: Two features - where the logic comes from and how a system handles something new - let you classify any everyday system as rule-based or learning.
objectives: Distinguish a rule-based system from a learning system using two clear features.
Give one everyday example of each and explain the difference.
Use the terms rule-based, learning, data and model accurately.

body: Two machines can do the same job in totally different ways. Today you learn the two features that reveal which is which - and you will never be fooled by a shiny screen again.

terms.definition: Logic written by a person as fixed steps.
A system that builds a model from data instead of fixed rules.
The labelled examples a learning system is shown.
The pattern a learning system builds from its data.
A true characteristic you use to classify a system, not a surface look.

sections.heading: Two features that decide it
body: **Feature one** - where does the logic come from? In a [[rule-based system]] a person writes it. In a [[learning system]] it comes from data.
**Feature two** - what happens with something new? A rule-based system only handles cases its rules cover. A learning system can handle new cases that look like its examples.

sections.heading: Data is not the model
body: Be careful with words. The [[data]] is the examples. The [[model]] is the pattern built from them. Change the data and you can change the model.
A learning system does not understand meaning - it matches patterns. Always check its answers.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Build the feature chart, then use it to classify everyday systems you meet in the UAE.
items: Add an example to each row.
Underline the feature that decided each answer.
Write two sentences using data and model correctly.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which feature is the strongest proof of a learning system?
Why is 'it looks modern' not a good reason?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the two features you now use to classify systems.
Write one system you are still unsure about and why.

worksheet.title: Week 2 Core worksheet - Rules vs Learning - How Each System Works

questions.prompt: Feature chart. Complete the chart with a feature and an example for each system type.
questions.stem:
Rule-based: logic comes from ___
Learning: logic comes from ___
questions.lookFor: Both rows name a non-surface feature - that in a rule-based system a person writes the logic, and in a learning system the logic comes from data - and each row carries an example. Watch for surface traits such as 'it looks modern' standing in for a feature.

questions.prompt: Classify and justify. Classify two systems and underline the deciding feature.
questions.lookFor: Classifies both examples correctly with a feature reason: a metro ticket gate is rule-based because a person set fixed rules, and a voice assistant that improves with use is learning because it builds a model from data and handles new phrases. Approaching: one classified correctly, or a surface trait mixed in.

questions.prompt: Classification record. Record each system, your classification, and the deciding feature.
questions.lookFor: Each row pairs a classification with a deciding feature rather than a surface look. The deciding-feature column should say where the logic comes from or how the system handles a new case.

questions.prompt: Exit ticket. Classify two systems your teacher names and give the feature that separates them.
questions.lookFor: Secure: classifies both correctly and names a distinguishing feature that is not a surface trait. Sort exit slips secure / partial / not-yet; if under 70 percent distinguish correctly, re-teach with the two-column feature chart.

questions.prompt: Challenge (stretch). Find a system that is genuinely hard to classify and argue both sides using features.
questions.lookFor: Argues both sides using the two features - where the logic comes from, and how the system handles a new case - rather than surface traits. This is the stretch task for students who already classify securely.
